concepts.title: CloudWatch: Metrics, Logs, and Alarms
concepts.description: CloudWatch is AWS's built-in observability service. Metrics tell you what is happening in aggregate, logs tell you what happened in detail, and alarms turn either into an automated reaction. Treating them as one undifferentiated 'monitoring' blob is how teams end up flying blind or drowning in noise.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between a CloudWatch metric and a CloudWatch log, and when each is the right tool to reach for.
Describe how metrics are structured (namespace, dimensions, statistic, period) and how that structure enables aggregation and filtering.
Explain the difference between AWS-published metrics (e.g. EC2 CPUUtilization) and custom/agent-collected metrics (e.g. memory usage), and why some 'obvious' metrics require an agent.
Read a Logs Insights query well enough to explain what it computes from raw log lines.
Explain how an alarm's period, evaluation periods, and datapoints-to-alarm settings interact to decide when it actually fires.
Explain why Average is often the wrong statistic for latency, and when a percentile statistic is the better choice.

sections.heading: Metrics: Numbers Sampled Over Time
sections.body:
A CloudWatch **metric** is a time-ordered series of data points for something you (or AWS) chose to measure: CPUUtilization, RequestCount, ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, and thousands of others. Every metric lives in a **namespace** (a grouping like `AWS/EC2` or `AWS/RDS` that keeps different services' metrics from colliding) and is further identified by **dimensions**, key/value pairs like `InstanceId=i-0abc123` that distinguish 'CPUUtilization for this instance' from 'CPUUtilization for that other instance' even though both share a name and namespace. When you graph or alarm on a metric, you query a namespace, metric name, and dimension combination, aggregated over a chosen **period** (the time bucket: 1 minute, 5 minutes, 1 hour) with a chosen **statistic** (Average, Sum, Maximum, Minimum, or a percentile like p99).

Most AWS services publish a baseline set of metrics automatically. EC2 publishes CPUUtilization, network, and disk I/O counters every 5 minutes by default (every minute if you enable detailed monitoring, at extra cost). The common surprise is that **EC2 does not publish memory utilization, disk space used, or any metric that requires looking inside the guest operating system**, because the hypervisor can't see inside the instance's OS, only the OS itself can observe how much RAM is in use. Getting that data into CloudWatch means installing the **CloudWatch agent** on the instance, which pushes OS-level readings as custom metrics. This trips up almost everyone the first time they look for a memory graph on a new EC2 instance and find nothing, not a flat line at zero but an absent metric, because nothing has ever published it.

sections.heading: Logs: What Actually Happened, Not Just the Aggregate
sections.body:
Where metrics answer 'how much, how many, over time', **CloudWatch Logs** answers 'what exactly happened, in what order'. Applications and services write log lines into a **log group** (a named container, typically one per application or Lambda function), and a **log stream** within it represents one source of lines: one EC2 instance, one Lambda execution environment, one ECS task. Log data arrives as raw text (or structured JSON if your application logs that way) and, unlike a metric, isn't pre-aggregated into a number. You query it afterward with **CloudWatch Logs Insights**, a query language that looks a little like SQL crossed with a Unix pipeline:

```text
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| stats count(*) as errorCount by bin(5m)
| sort errorCount desc
```

This query scans a log group's raw lines, keeps the ones containing `ERROR`, buckets them into 5-minute windows, counts each bucket, and sorts by count. It turns unstructured text into the time-series view a metric would give natively, computed on demand from the raw logs instead of pre-aggregated as the data arrived.

One detail is a real cost trap: **log groups default to Never Expire retention**. Every line an application writes accumulates in the log group forever, at CloudWatch Logs' per-GB storage price, until someone sets a retention period (1 week, 1 month, 1 year, and options between). A chatty application logging at DEBUG in production, left on the default for a year, becomes a significant and avoidable line item. Set an explicit retention policy on every log group when you create it, matched to how long the data is useful for debugging or compliance. Ingestion is billed too, so the volume you write matters as much as how long you keep it.

sections.heading: Alarms: Turning a Metric Into an Automatic Reaction
sections.body:
A CloudWatch **alarm** watches a single metric (or a math expression combining several) and moves between three states: **OK** (the metric is behaving), **ALARM** (it has breached the threshold), and **INSUFFICIENT_DATA** (CloudWatch doesn't have enough recent datapoints to evaluate the alarm, a distinct and calmer state, common right after an alarm is created or after a resource stops reporting, such as a terminated instance).

Three settings work together to decide when an alarm fires, and getting the combination wrong is a common source of both false alarms and missed real ones: **period** (the size of each evaluation bucket -- e.g. 60 seconds), **evaluation periods** (how many of the most recent buckets to look at -- e.g. 5), and **datapoints to alarm** (how many of those evaluated buckets actually need to breach the threshold to trigger ALARM -- e.g. 3 out of 5). Setting evaluation periods and datapoints to alarm equal (5 of 5) makes the alarm strict and slow, requiring a sustained breach across the whole window. That avoids noise from a single spike but is slower to report a real ongoing problem. Setting datapoints to alarm lower than evaluation periods (3 of 5) makes the alarm catch an intermittent, flapping condition without demanding a continuous breach, which often suits noisy real-world metrics that dip in and out of a bad state.

An alarm also has a setting for how it treats missing data (`missing`, `notBreaching`, `breaching`, or `ignore`). This matters for a metric that a dead or terminated instance simply stops reporting. The default is `missing`, under which the alarm eventually goes to INSUFFICIENT_DATA, which doesn't notify anyone unless you attach an action to that state. With `notBreaching`, which many people choose to reduce noise, an instance that goes completely dark, the worst outcome, leaves the alarm calmly in OK, because there is no data to evaluate as a breach. Check this setting for any alarm meant to catch total failure, not just degraded performance. `breaching` is the usual choice for a signal that must keep arriving.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes: The Wrong Statistic, and Averages That Hide Problems
sections.body:
Making **Average** the default statistic is a natural habit and often the wrong choice for the metrics people care about most, with request latency the classic case. If 99 requests out of 100 complete in 50ms and one takes 5 seconds, the average is about 99ms, which hides the one request a user experienced as a 5-second hang. Percentile statistics (p90, p99, p99.9) surface this tail behavior: p99 is the latency that 1% of requests exceed, a different and usually more actionable question than 'what's the mean'. As a rule, use Average or Sum for capacity-style metrics where the aggregate is what matters (total bytes transferred, total request count), and use a percentile, usually p99 or higher, for anything latency-related, where a small fraction of bad outcomes is exactly what you want to catch and an average washes it out.

A related mistake is a period too coarse for the thing measured: a 1-hour period on a metric that spikes for 10 minutes averages the spike below the threshold, so the alarm never fires although users had a real problem for 10 minutes. Matching the period to how fast the condition changes, and using a percentile instead of a mean when tail behavior matters, serve one discipline: make sure the number the alarm evaluates still resembles what you set out to detect, not an aggregation that erases it.

examples.title: A CloudWatch Logs Insights Query for Error-Rate Spikes
examples.code:
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| stats count(*) as errorCount by bin(5m)
| sort errorCount desc
| limit 20
examples.explanation: This query scans a log group's raw lines instead of reading a pre-aggregated number. `filter @message like /ERROR/` discards every line that doesn't match `ERROR`, `stats count(*) as errorCount by bin(5m)` groups the remaining lines into 5-minute buckets and counts each, `sort errorCount desc` puts the noisiest windows first, and `limit 20` caps the output. Logs answer a question metrics can't on their own. An alarm can tell you the error rate rose, and Logs Insights gets you from 'something was wrong around 2:15pm' to the error lines in that five-minute window (rerun the query with the time range narrowed and the `stats` line removed to see the raw lines), computed on demand without the error rate ever having been published as a metric.

examples.title: Alarming on p99 Latency Instead of Average
examples.explanation: `--extended-statistic "p99"` (instead of `--statistic Average`) makes the alarm evaluate the response time of the slowest 1% of requests in each period, which keeps a rare but real tail-latency problem from being averaged away. `--period 60` with `--evaluation-periods 5` and `--datapoints-to-alarm 3` has the alarm look at the five most recent 60-second buckets and fire when at least three show p99 above the 1.0 second threshold, quick enough to catch an ongoing problem within minutes without firing on one noisy minute. `--treat-missing-data notBreaching` means silence from the load balancer isn't counted as a breach, reasonable here but worth revisiting for an alarm meant to catch total outages (an ALB with no traffic also reports no latency datapoints).

examples.title: Publishing a Custom Application Metric CloudWatch Doesn't Know About
examples.explanation: AWS-published metrics cover only what AWS's services know internally. Nothing in EC2 or CloudWatch can know how many jobs sit in an application-defined queue, because that number exists only in the application's logic. `put_metric_data` is how an application pushes an arbitrary number, under a namespace it chooses (`MyApp/Queues` here, distinct from any AWS namespace), as a custom metric that can then be graphed and alarmed on like `CPUUtilization`, with the same statistics, periods, and alarms. It is the general escape hatch for 'CloudWatch has no metric for the thing I care about'. Custom metrics are billed per metric per month, and every distinct dimension combination counts as a separate metric, so publish deliberately for important signals and avoid high-cardinality dimensions such as user IDs. (This example needs AWS credentials and a Region configured, which is why it can't run standalone.)

misconceptions.description: If CloudWatch isn't showing a metric like memory utilization for my EC2 instance, that must mean memory usage is fine.
misconceptions.clarification: EC2 does not publish memory, disk space, or any other guest-OS-level metric by default, because the hypervisor has no visibility inside the instance's operating system, only the OS itself can observe that. An absent metric means nothing has been configured to collect and publish it (typically the CloudWatch agent), not that the value is healthy. A missing graph is a monitoring gap, not a clean bill of health.
misconceptions.fact: EC2 does not publish memory, disk space, or any other guest-OS-level metric by default, because the hypervisor has no visibility inside the instance's operating system -- only the OS itself can observe that.

misconceptions.description: An alarm in state INSUFFICIENT_DATA means something is broken and needs immediate attention, the same as ALARM.
misconceptions.clarification: INSUFFICIENT_DATA means CloudWatch doesn't have enough recent datapoints to evaluate the alarm, which is common right after an alarm is created or when a resource has stopped reporting (for example, because it was terminated on purpose). It is distinct from ALARM, which means the metric was evaluated and found breaching. Treating the two identically causes needless panic over routine situations (a brand-new alarm with no history) or, worse, trains people to ignore INSUFFICIENT_DATA notifications that sometimes do signal a real problem, like an instance that stopped reporting because it crashed.

exercises.prompt: Given this alarm configuration and CPU utilization timeline, determine which minute the alarm first transitions from OK to ALARM, and explain why.
exercises.code:
alarm config: period=60s, evaluation_periods=5, datapoints_to_alarm=3, threshold=80 (GreaterThanThreshold), statistic=Average

minute  CPUUtilization
1       55
2       82   (breach)
3       60
4       85   (breach)
5       88   (breach)
6       90   (breach)
hints: The alarm doesn't require 5 CONSECUTIVE breaching minutes -- it requires 3 breaching datapoints among the most recent 5 evaluated periods.
At each minute, ask: looking back across the most recent 5 one-minute periods (or fewer, if the alarm hasn't existed that long), how many of them breached 80?
Count breaches within the rolling 5-minute window ending at minute 5, not the whole timeline at once.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The alarm fires at minute 5. In the window of the 5 most recent periods (minutes 1-5), minutes 2, 4, and 5 breach: exactly 3 breaching datapoints, which meets datapoints_to_alarm=3. It does not fire earlier (only 2 breaches existed by minute 4) and minute 6 is irrelevant because the alarm had already fired.
exercises.solutionExplanation: datapoints_to_alarm=3 out of evaluation_periods=5 means CloudWatch evaluates a sliding window of the 5 most recent periods and checks whether at least 3 breached the threshold; they need not be consecutive. At minute 4 the window (only minutes 1-4 exist so far) contains breaches at minutes 2 and 4, only 2. At minute 5 the window of minutes 1-5 contains breaches at 2, 4, and 5, exactly 3, so the alarm fires at minute 5. (This assumes the alarm existed and reported from minute 1, so the earliest datapoints are not treated as missing.) Minute 6's breach doesn't change when the alarm first fired.

exercises.prompt: A metric filter is supposed to count how many log lines represent a failed payment, but it never matches anything, even though the application logs failures constantly. Find and fix the bug.
hints: A CloudWatch Logs metric filter pattern with space-separated terms requires each literal term to actually appear in the log line -- check whether every term in the pattern is actually present.
Look closely at the log level the application actually logs failed payments at, versus the level the pattern requires.
The goal is to match lines representing a failed payment -- does the pattern need to depend on a specific log level term at all to achieve that?
exercises.solutionCode:
// Fixed metric filter pattern -- matches on the term that's actually guaranteed present
"payment_failed"
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original pattern `"ERROR payment_failed"` is a quoted phrase, so a line must contain that exact text, and unquoted space-separated terms would instead require every term to appear. Either way the application logs failed payments at `[WARN]`, not `[ERROR]`, so `ERROR` never appears and the filter matches zero lines despite constant failures. The fix drops the dependency on a log-level term that doesn't reflect reality and matches on `payment_failed`, the term present whenever this failure occurs. Metric filter patterns match literal text, not intent, so check an actual sample log line, not just the code that appears to produce it, before trusting a pattern's assumptions about level or wording. (You can test a pattern against sample lines in the console or with `aws logs test-metric-filter` before creating it.)

assessments.prompt: An API's average response time looks healthy at 120ms, but a growing number of user complaints describe multi-second hangs. Which change to the monitoring setup is most likely to actually surface this problem?
options: Switch the metric's namespace to a custom namespace so it can be graphed separately.
Switch the alarm's statistic from Average to a high percentile like p99.
Increase the alarm's period from 60 seconds to 1 hour so it has more data to average over.
Lower the alarm threshold on the existing Average-based latency alarm.
assessments.explanation: A small number of slow requests mixed into many fast ones is the scenario Average is bad at surfacing: the mean moves only slightly for a handful of outliers, while a percentile like p99 reports what the slowest fraction of requests experienced. Lowering the threshold on an Average-based alarm (“Lower the alarm threshold on the existing…”) doesn't fix the underlying blind spot; the average was never going to spike enough to cross a reasonable threshold in the first place. Increasing the period (“Increase the alarm's period from 60 seconds…”) makes the problem worse, not better, by averaging over an even larger, more diluting window. Changing the namespace (“Switch the metric's namespace to a custom…”) is purely organizational and has no effect on which statistic is being evaluated.

assessments.prompt: A team launches a brand-new EC2 instance and looks in CloudWatch for a memory-utilization graph. They find nothing at all -- not a flat line at zero, no metric exists whatsoever. What does this most likely indicate?
options: EC2 does not publish guest-OS-level metrics like memory utilization by default.
The chosen instance type doesn't support memory monitoring; switching to a different instance family would make the metric appear automatically.
Memory usage is currently at exactly 0%, so CloudWatch has nothing meaningful to graph yet.
Memory metrics simply take up to 24 hours to begin appearing after an instance's first launch.
assessments.explanation: An absent metric, not a flat zero line but no data series at all, means nothing has been configured to collect and publish that value. That is the case for memory utilization on EC2: the hypervisor can't see inside the guest OS, so AWS never publishes it by default the way it does CPUUtilization. The CloudWatch agent, installed and run on the instance, is what surfaces the data. The “Memory usage is currently at exactly 0%…” option misreads an absent metric as a data point, when it's the complete absence of one. The “Memory metrics simply take up to 24…” option invents a delay that isn't the actual cause. The “The chosen instance type doesn't support memory…” option fabricates an instance-family-based restriction that doesn't exist -- the agent requirement applies uniformly regardless of instance type.

assessments.prompt: A team notices their CloudWatch Logs bill has grown steadily every month for over a year, even though daily request volume and daily log line count have stayed essentially flat. What is the most likely explanation?
options: CloudWatch Logs charges retroactively for an entire year's worth of logs once a log group crosses a size threshold.
CloudWatch Logs pricing increases automatically over time regardless of actual usage.
This pattern indicates a memory leak in the application causing increasingly verbose log lines each month.

Log groups default to Never Expire retention, so every day's log lines accumulate indefinitely at CloudWatch Logs' per-GB storage price unless an explicit retention period is set -- a flat daily log volume still means the total amount of stored data, and therefore storage cost, keeps growing every month.
assessments.explanation: Log groups default to Never Expire retention, so nothing is deleted unless someone sets a retention period. Even with a flat daily log volume, the cumulative stored total grows every month, and storage cost grows with it. The “CloudWatch Logs pricing increases automatically over time…” option invents a pricing mechanism that doesn't exist. The “This pattern indicates a memory leak…” option assumes a code-level cause when the described symptom (flat daily volume) explicitly rules out growing per-day verbosity. The “CloudWatch Logs charges retroactively for an entire…” option fabricates a retroactive billing behavior that isn't how CloudWatch Logs pricing works -- storage is billed continuously as data accumulates, not retroactively triggered by a threshold.

assessments.prompt: An alarm on a health-check metric is configured with treat-missing-data set to notBreaching. The monitored instance crashes entirely and stops reporting the metric altogether. What is the likely, and potentially dangerous, consequence?
options: The alarm immediately transitions to ALARM, since notBreaching treats any missing data as an automatic breach of the threshold.
CloudWatch deletes the alarm outright once its monitored resource stops reporting data for more than an hour.
The alarm may remain in OK or INSUFFICIENT_DATA rather than firing.
CloudWatch automatically switches the alarm's missing-data treatment to breaching after five minutes with no data.
assessments.explanation: notBreaching means missing data is treated as if the metric were fine, not as a breach, so a total failure that stops the metric from being reported can leave the alarm sitting in OK or INSUFFICIENT_DATA instead of firing, the opposite of what you want from an alarm meant to catch a crashed instance. The “The alarm immediately transitions to ALARM, since…” option describes the opposite setting's behavior (breaching), not notBreaching. The “CloudWatch automatically switches the alarm's missing-data treatment…” and “CloudWatch deletes the alarm outright once…” options both invent automatic behavior changes that CloudWatch does not perform -- the configured missing-data treatment stays fixed unless someone explicitly changes it, and alarms are not auto-deleted for going quiet.

assessments.prompt: Explain how an alarm's period, evaluation periods, and datapoints-to-alarm settings interact, and why misconfiguring them can cause both false positives (noisy pages for transient blips) and false negatives (missing a real, ongoing problem).
assessments.modelAnswer: An alarm's period is the size of each bucket of aggregated metric data, say 60 seconds. Evaluation periods is how many of the most recent buckets CloudWatch looks at when deciding whether to fire, say 5, meaning the last 5 minutes at a 60-second period. Datapoints to alarm is how many of those buckets must breach the threshold for the alarm to enter ALARM, say 3. Together they form a sliding window with a threshold count, not a simple 'is the metric over X right now' check: CloudWatch re-evaluates the most recent N buckets (N = evaluation periods) on each new datapoint and fires once at least M of them (M = datapoints to alarm) have breached. Setting M equal to N (5 of 5) demands a sustained breach across the whole window, which avoids false positives from a single spike but is slower to report a real ongoing problem, since every bucket has to be bad. Setting M below N (3 of 5) makes the alarm more sensitive to an intermittent, flapping condition, firing even if the metric dips in and out of breach, which often matches real noisy metrics but can let a few unrelated transient spikes scattered across the window trigger a page. Both directions of error cost something. Too strict (M close to N, or a coarse period that averages spikes away) gives false negatives, missing real problems that aren't perfectly sustained. Too loose (M much smaller than N, or a very short period reacting to normal noise) gives false positives, paging on blips that resolve themselves and teaching whoever is on call to stop trusting the alarm.

concepts.title: Alerting Without Alert Fatigue
concepts.description: A monitoring system that pages a human for everything eventually trains that human to ignore it. Designing alerts around what requires action, not around what CloudWatch can measure, keeps an on-call rotation responsive when something real breaks.
learningObjectives: Explain why alert fatigue is a predictable, structural consequence of paging on every anomaly rather than every actionable condition.

Distinguish symptom-based alerting (user-facing impact) from cause-based alerting (internal metric anomalies), and explain why symptom-based alerts should page while cause-based signals usually shouldn't.
Design a basic alert severity tiering scheme (page vs ticket vs dashboard-only) and match each tier to an appropriate notification channel.
Explain how composite alarms and anomaly detection reduce noisy single-metric alarms into fewer, more meaningful signals.
Explain why an alert's content -- not just its existence -- affects how quickly a real incident gets resolved.

sections.heading: Alert Fatigue Is a Predictable, Structural Failure Mode
sections.body: It feels safer to alarm on everything CloudWatch can measure, since more coverage sounds like it can only help. In practice this backfires, and not through carelessness: it is a predictable consequence of how people respond to a high volume of low-value interruptions. An on-call engineer who gets a dozen pages a week for harmless conditions (a CPU blip during a known nightly batch job, a metric that crossed a threshold and recovered on its own) can't treat each with full urgency indefinitely. They habituate: glance at the page, recognize 'oh, that one again', and dismiss it without investigating. Habituation doesn't apply only to the noisy alarms. It dulls the response to *all* pages from that channel, including the rare one that is a real, novel incident. 'Be more disciplined about checking every page' fights basic human attention. The fix is to stop sending pages that don't warrant full urgency, so a page reliably means something.

sections.heading: Symptom-Based vs Cause-Based Alerting
sections.body:
A **symptom-based** alert fires on something a user or the business would notice or be harmed by: an elevated 5xx rate on a customer-facing endpoint, checkout latency high enough to hurt conversion, an availability drop on the login flow. A **cause-based** alert fires on an internal condition that might or might not be contributing to a symptom: CPU at 85%, memory climbing, queue depth trending up. A cause-based signal can be correct and still not warrant a page, because many causes never produce a user-visible symptom (a batch job pegs CPU at 85% every night at 2am with no customer impact), and because a real symptom can have causes nobody predicted or instrumented.

So reserve paging, which interrupts a person day or night and demands action within minutes, for symptom-based conditions close to user or business impact. Cause-based metrics stay valuable, just not as page triggers: they belong on dashboards, in lower-urgency tickets, or as context a responder pulls up to diagnose *why* a symptom is happening. It is the discipline behind choosing p99 over Average in the previous concept: match the signal you act on to what you care about, not to what was easiest to measure.

sections.heading: Tiering Severity and Routing Alerts Appropriately
sections.body:
A workable alerting scheme has at least three tiers, each with its own channel and expected response time, instead of sending everything to one pager. **Page** goes to an on-call rotation (through something like PagerDuty or an SNS topic wired to a paging integration), is expected to be acted on within minutes, and is reserved for symptom-based, user-impacting conditions. **Ticket** creates a tracked work item for business-hours follow-up, suited to a cause-based trend worth investigating soon but not urgently, like disk usage climbing toward a limit weeks out. **Dashboard-only** is visible when someone looks and never pushed to anyone, suited to routine metrics that give context but aren't anomalies on their own.

A related technique that reduces noise without reducing coverage is the **composite alarm**. Instead of three alarms independently paging for elevated error rate, elevated latency, and a drop in healthy hosts (three pages for what is probably one event), a composite alarm combines alarm states with AND/OR logic and enters ALARM, and pages, only when the combination indicates a real incident, such as elevated errors *and* a drop in healthy hosts. That cuts the pages for one incident from three to one without silencing any underlying signal, which stays available on a dashboard for diagnosis.

sections.heading: Runbooks and Actionable Alert Content
sections.body:
An alert's *existence* is half of what makes it useful. Its *content* determines how quickly the recipient can act. A page that says only 'ALARM: HighErrorRate' forces the person paged to rebuild context from scratch at 3am: which service, which dashboard, what is the normal baseline, has this happened before, what to check first. A well-designed alert includes or links the dashboard for the affected service, the relevant runbook (a short, maintained document with the first diagnostic steps and known common causes for this alarm), and enough detail in the text (which metric, which threshold, current value) that the responder doesn't have to hunt for the basics. The alarm's description field and SNS message are the places to put this.

The cost of a page isn't only whether it fires appropriately but how long the recipient takes to go from 'woken by a notification' to 'diagnosing the right thing'. An alert that shortens that gap improves response time even for a rare incident, which is the point of paging.

examples.title: A Composite Alarm Turning Three Flapping Alarms Into One Meaningful Page
examples.explanation: Instead of two independent alarms, one on elevated 5xx rate and one on a drop in healthy target-group hosts, each paging separately, this composite alarm enters ALARM only when *both* underlying alarms are in ALARM at once. A brief 5xx blip with healthy hosts (often self-recovering) no longer pages, and neither does a healthy-host dip from a routine deploy cycling instances. Both conditions together are a much stronger signal of a real outage and produce one page for that incident, instead of two noisier alarms firing and re-firing throughout it. The underlying alarms should have no `--alarm-actions` of their own, or they will still page individually.

examples.title: Symptom-Based vs Cause-Based Alarm Configuration, Side by Side
examples.code:
# Symptom-based: pages, because it's close to real user impact
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "checkout-5xx-rate-high" \
  --namespace "AWS/ApplicationELB" --metric-name "HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count" \
  --statistic Sum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 2 \
  --threshold 10 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:oncall-alerts

# Cause-based: dashboard-only, no paging action attached
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "checkout-instance-cpu-elevated" \
  --namespace "AWS/EC2" --metric-name "CPUUtilization" \
  --dimensions Name=AutoScalingGroupName,Value=checkout-asg \
  --statistic Average --period 300 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 3 \
  --threshold 75 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold
examples.explanation: Both alarms are worth having but serve different purposes. The first watches the 5xx count on the customer-facing checkout endpoint, a direct symptom of user impact, and its `--alarm-actions` point at the on-call SNS topic, so it pages. The second watches EC2 CPU on the same service's instances, a possible cause but not a guarantee of any user-visible problem, since the autoscaling group may be handling normal load fine. It deliberately has no `--alarm-actions`, so it still moves between OK and ALARM and shows on a CloudWatch dashboard but never interrupts anyone. If checkout errors later spike, this alarm's history is the cause-based context someone pulls up while investigating the page.

examples.title: Anomaly Detection Instead of a Static Threshold for a Seasonal Metric
examples.code:
aws cloudwatch put-anomaly-detector \
  --namespace "AWS/ApplicationELB" --metric-name "RequestCount" \
  --dimensions Name=LoadBalancer,Value=app/my-alb/1234567890abcdef \
  --stat Sum

# The alarm takes the metric and the expected band as metric math in a file;
# --namespace/--statistic/--period are not allowed alongside --metrics.
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "request-count-anomalous" \
  --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 2 \
  --comparison-operator LessThanLowerOrGreaterThanUpperThreshold \
  --threshold-metric-id ad1 \
  --metrics file://anomaly-metrics.json \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:oncall-alerts

# anomaly-metrics.json
# [
#   { "Id": "m1", "ReturnData": true,
#     "MetricStat": { "Metric": { "Namespace": "AWS/ApplicationELB", "MetricName": "RequestCount",
#       "Dimensions": [{ "Name": "LoadBalancer", "Value": "app/my-alb/1234567890abcdef" }] },
#       "Period": 300, "Stat": "Sum" } },
#   { "Id": "ad1", "Expression": "ANOMALY_DETECTION_BAND(m1, 2)", "Label": "RequestCount expected band", "ReturnData": true }
# ]
examples.explanation: Traffic to a typical web service is rarely flat: higher in business hours and on weekdays, lower overnight and on weekends. A single static threshold must choose between two bad options. Set low enough to catch a real overnight drop, it fires every night as quiet hours begin. Set low enough to survive the normal overnight dip, it is too loose to catch a real drop during business hours, when the same request count would be alarming. CloudWatch anomaly detection learns the metric's normal range as a band that varies by time of day and day of week, and the alarm fires only when the value leaves that band. A normal 2am dip stays inside the correspondingly lower band, while a real drop or spike at any hour does fire. This escapes the false-positive versus false-negative trade a static threshold can't. Note the alarm compares the metric with the band through a metric math expression, which is why the command takes a `--metrics` file instead of `--statistic` and `--period`, and the detector needs some days of data before its band is useful.

misconceptions.description: The safest alerting strategy is to alarm on every metric available, since more monitoring coverage can only help.
misconceptions.clarification: Paging on every available signal degrades the signal-to-noise ratio of the paging channel, until a real, urgent page gets the same dulled, delayed response as routine noise. This is a well-documented attention effect, not a discipline failure on the responder's part. The fix isn't less monitoring coverage but routing most of it to dashboards and tickets, and reserving pages for symptom-based, user-impacting conditions.

misconceptions.description: A static-threshold alarm and an anomaly-detection alarm are basically interchangeable ways to alert on the same metric.
misconceptions.clarification: A static threshold doesn't account for a metric's expected variation over time (daily or weekly seasonality). It is either loose enough to survive normal peaks and troughs, and so misses real problems in a normally quiet period, or tight enough to catch them and so fires constantly during normal peaks or troughs. Anomaly detection models the expected band of normal values, which moves with time-of-day and day-of-week patterns, and alerts on deviation from it. It is a different mechanism, suited to seasonal metrics that one fixed number can't represent.

exercises.prompt: An on-call engineer has started silencing pages from their phone overnight because they're paged roughly 30 times a week, and nearly all of those pages turn out to be a CPUUtilization alarm firing every night during a known, harmless data-warehouse batch job. Diagnose the design problem with this alerting setup and propose a fix.
exercises.code:
alarm: nightly-batch-cpu-high
metric: AWS/EC2 CPUUtilization, AutoScalingGroupName=batch-asg
threshold: > 70% average, period=300s, evaluation_periods=3, datapoints_to_alarm=3
action: pages on-call via SNS -> PagerDuty, every single night around 1am
hints: Ask whether this alarm is symptom-based (something a user would notice) or cause-based (an internal condition that may or may not matter) -- and what that implies about whether it should page at all.
The batch job's CPU usage being high every night is described as expected and harmless -- does an expected, harmless condition need to interrupt a human in real time?

Consider what should actually page here instead: is there a more direct signal of the batch job genuinely failing or overrunning, rather than a proxy metric (CPU) that happens to correlate with it running normally?
exercises.solutionCode:
# Remove the paging action from the CPU alarm entirely -- keep it as a dashboard-only signal
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name nightly-batch-cpu-high ... # (no --alarm-actions)

# Add a symptom-based alarm on the actual thing that matters: did the batch job fail or run too long
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "nightly-batch-job-failed-or-overran" \
  --namespace "MyApp/BatchJobs" --metric-name "JobDurationMinutes" \
  --statistic Maximum --period 300 --evaluation-periods 1 --datapoints-to-alarm 1 \
  --threshold 120 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --treat-missing-data breaching \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:oncall-alerts
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original alarm uses a cause-based signal (elevated CPU) as if it were a symptom. High CPU during this job is expected and never itself a problem, and the alarm fires every night purely because the job runs successfully, which produces the habituation and silencing in the scenario. The fix removes the paging action from the CPU alarm (it can stay as a dashboard signal) and moves the page to a symptom-based signal: a custom metric the batch job publishes with its own duration, alarmed on exceeding the expected runtime. `--treat-missing-data breaching` means a job that never reports a duration at all (because it crashed outright) also pages, instead of being ignored as 'no data'. One caveat: with a once-per-night metric and a 300-second period, most periods have no datapoint, so `breaching` would alarm all day. Using a longer period (for example 24 hours) or publishing a heartbeat metric avoids that.

exercises.prompt: Write a CloudWatch composite alarm (as an AWS CLI command) that pages only when BOTH an elevated 5xx error rate alarm ('api-5xx-high') AND a low healthy-host-count alarm ('api-healthy-hosts-low') are simultaneously in ALARM, instead of paging separately for each.
hints: The --alarm-rule expression uses ALARM("alarm-name") as a boolean building block, combined with AND/OR/NOT.
The composite alarm itself needs its own --alarm-actions pointed at the SNS topic -- the underlying two alarms don't need paging actions of their own if only the composite should page.
Give the composite alarm a name that describes the combined condition, distinct from either underlying alarm's name.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The `--alarm-rule` expression `ALARM("api-5xx-high") AND ALARM("api-healthy-hosts-low")` means the composite alarm enters ALARM only when both underlying alarms, evaluated independently, are in ALARM together. Either alone (a brief error blip with healthy hosts, or a host-count dip during a routine deploy) is not enough. Only the composite carries `--alarm-actions`, so the two underlying alarms stay visible and trackable for diagnosis but no longer page on their own, collapsing up to two pages for one incident into one without losing any signal.

assessments.prompt: A team is deciding which of two conditions should page an on-call engineer: (1) checkout page error rate exceeding 2% for 3 minutes, or (2) database CPU utilization exceeding 60%. Which is the better candidate for paging, and why?
options: Database CPU exceeding 60%, because catching a cause early prevents it from ever becoming a symptom.
Neither should page; both should be dashboard-only, since paging should be reserved exclusively for full outages, and neither of these conditions describes a service that is completely unreachable.
Checkout error rate exceeding 2%, because it is a symptom directly tied to user-facing impact, whereas elevated database CPU may or may not ever translate into a real problem.
Both should page, since more coverage during an incident is always better than less.
assessments.explanation: Checkout error rate is a symptom-based signal that reflects what a real user experiences now, which is worth interrupting a human for. Database CPU at 60% is a cause-based signal that often corresponds to no user-facing problem (a database can run comfortably at 60% CPU indefinitely), and using it as a page trigger invites the alert fatigue described earlier. The “Database CPU exceeding 60%, because catching…” option gets the direction backwards -- elevated CPU catching a 'cause early' sounds appealing but produces far more false-positive pages than genuine early warnings, since most CPU elevation never actually becomes a symptom. The “Both should page, since more coverage during…” option ignores that indiscriminate paging degrades response quality for everything, including real incidents. The “Neither should page; both should be dashboard-only…” option overcorrects -- symptom-based alerts like a real checkout error-rate spike are exactly what paging exists for, not something to demote to dashboard-only.

assessments.prompt: A team reasons: 'Even if we page for lots of low-value conditions, our on-call engineers are professionals -- they'll just triage carefully and give full attention to the real incidents whenever they occur.' What does this reasoning get wrong about how alert fatigue actually works?
options: Alert fatigue only affects pages sent outside business hours, so this concern doesn't apply to daytime paging.

Habituation from frequent low-value pages doesn't selectively spare the rare real incident -- it dulls the response to all pages arriving from that same channel, including genuinely urgent ones, as a predictable consequence of ordinary human attention economics rather than a discipline failure on the responder's part.
Nothing; disciplined engineers can reliably maintain full, undiminished attention to every single page regardless of how many low-value pages preceded it.
This reasoning is correct as long as the team rotates on-call engineers frequently enough to avoid burnout.
assessments.explanation: Habituation to noise doesn't discriminate: a responder trained by a dozen harmless pages a week to expect 'oh, that one again' can't suspend that response only for the one page that is real, since there is no way to tell it apart in advance. It is a structural, predictable consequence of how attention works, not a matter of individual discipline or professionalism. The “Nothing; disciplined engineers can reliably maintain full…” option assumes an ability to resist habituation that isn't realistic at any sustained volume of low-value interruptions. The “This reasoning is correct as long…” and “Alert fatigue only affects pages sent outside…” options both invent conditions (rotation frequency, time of day) that don't address the actual mechanism, which applies regardless of either factor.

assessments.prompt: A team sets a static alarm threshold on request count low enough that it never fires during the normal overnight traffic dip. What is the likely trade-off of setting the threshold this way?
options: The threshold automatically recalibrates itself to the correct level during business hours without any further configuration needed.
There is no trade-off; a threshold that survives the overnight dip without firing is simply the correct threshold, with no downside.
This trade-off only applies to metrics evaluated with the Sum statistic, not with Average.

The same threshold, set low enough to avoid firing during normal low-traffic hours, becomes too loose to reliably catch a genuine traffic drop during business hours, where that same absolute request count would actually represent a meaningful anomaly.
assessments.explanation: A single static threshold has to work across the metric's whole range of normal variation, and a metric with daily seasonality like request count has a very different normal at 3am and at 2pm. A number low enough to never trip during the overnight trough is too low to distinguish a real business-hours problem from ordinary traffic, since business-hours traffic sits well above it even when something is wrong. The “There is no trade-off; a threshold…” option ignores this seasonality mismatch entirely. The “The threshold automatically recalibrates itself…” option invents automatic recalibration that a plain static threshold does not have -- that adaptive behavior is specifically what anomaly detection provides instead. The “This trade-off only applies to metrics evaluated…” option is an arbitrary, unfounded restriction; the seasonality mismatch applies regardless of which statistic is chosen.

assessments.prompt: A new on-call rotation is being set up for a service that currently has a dozen CloudWatch alarms, most of them wired directly to page the on-call phone. Explain how you would redesign this into a paging strategy that avoids alert fatigue while still catching real incidents quickly.
assessments.modelAnswer: Start by auditing each alarm and classifying it as symptom-based (it reflects something a user or the business would notice: elevated customer-facing error rate, degraded checkout latency, an availability drop on a critical endpoint) or cause-based (an internal condition like CPU, memory, or queue depth that may or may not produce a symptom). Only symptom-based alarms keep a paging action. Every cause-based alarm loses its paging action and surfaces on a dashboard, or routes to a lower-urgency ticket if it is a trend worth investigating in business hours (disk usage climbing toward a limit weeks out) without waking anyone tonight. Where several related alarms tend to fire together for the same underlying incident -- elevated error rate, elevated latency, and a drop in healthy host count all spiking during the same outage -- a composite alarm combining them with AND/OR logic should replace the three individual pages with one, evaluated only when the combination genuinely indicates a real problem, while keeping each individual alarm visible on a dashboard for diagnosis. For any metric with genuine daily or weekly seasonality (traffic volume, request counts), a static threshold is likely to be either too loose to catch business-hours problems or too tight to survive normal overnight dips, so anomaly detection, which models the expected band of values as it naturally varies by time and day, is usually the better mechanism there. Finally, review the alert text and linked runbook of every alarm that still pages, asking whether someone woken at 3am can start diagnosing immediately without first reconstructing what the alarm means. The goal isn't fewer alarms for their own sake. It is that when the on-call phone rings, it reliably means something that needs a human now, which keeps the team responding quickly instead of dismissing pages out of habit.

concepts.title: Cost Optimization: Right-Sizing, Commitment Discounts, and Avoiding Bill Shock
concepts.description: AWS bills grow from a few well-understood patterns: over-provisioned resources, the wrong pricing model for a workload's predictability, and things nobody remembered to turn off. A few habits (utilization review, tagging, budgets, anomaly detection) catch most of the damage before an invoice does.
learningObjectives: Explain what right-sizing means and how to use utilization data, rather than guesses, to identify over-provisioned resources.
Distinguish On-Demand, Savings Plans/Reserved capacity, and Spot pricing at an account-management level, and explain the risk of over-committing to reserved capacity.
Explain the classic 'forgot to turn it off' bill-shock pattern and identify the concrete resource types most commonly responsible for it.
Explain the role of resource tagging in cost allocation, and why untagged spend becomes a governance blind spot.
Design a basic cost-guardrail setup combining budgets, anomaly detection, and automated non-production shutdown schedules.

sections.heading: Right-Sizing: Using Real Utilization Data, Not Guesses
sections.body:
**Right-sizing** means matching a resource's provisioned capacity to what it uses, based on observed data instead of a guess made before anyone had real load to look at. Teams commonly and understandably over-provision at launch: nobody wants to be the one who sized too small and caused an outage, so 'a bit bigger than we think we need' becomes the default, and once something works, revisiting the sizing never feels urgent. Across dozens or hundreds of resources, the fleet runs well below the utilization it was sized for, and the gap between provisioned and used capacity is waste paid for every hour.

The fix is mechanical: pull CloudWatch utilization metrics (CPU, and memory via the CloudWatch agent, as covered earlier) over a representative window, long enough to include normal peaks and not just a quiet afternoon, and compare them to the instance's capacity. AWS's **Compute Optimizer** does this across an account, analyzing historical utilization and recommending smaller instance types (or, just as importantly if less often, larger ones for something under-provisioned and struggling), with an estimated saving on each recommendation. (It needs the agent's memory metric to judge memory well, and some history of metrics to work from.) Right-sizing isn't limited to EC2. An RDS instance sized for a load spike that never came, or an EBS volume provisioned for far more IOPS than the workload uses, is the same pattern, and the same discipline applies: look at real utilization, not the original guess.

sections.heading: Commitment Discounts at Scale: Savings Plans and Reserved Capacity
sections.body:
For a single instance, choosing between On-Demand, Savings Plans/Reserved Instances, and Spot is a workload-fit decision covered earlier. Across an account or organization it becomes a portfolio decision, with a risk that doesn't appear for one instance: **over-commitment**. A Savings Plan or Reserved Instance is a financial commitment for a fixed term (1 or 3 years), sized against a forecast of steady usage, and if usage later drops (a service is decommissioned, a migration moves to a different instance family, a team scales down) the commitment doesn't shrink. You keep paying for committed capacity you no longer use, a different and in some ways worse waste than over-provisioning, because it is locked in for the rest of the term and can't be fixed by resizing an instance today. Compute Savings Plans are the more forgiving option, since they apply across instance families, sizes, and Regions, while EC2 Instance Savings Plans and Standard Reserved Instances are tied to a family.

The mitigation is twofold. Track **coverage** (the fraction of actual usage covered by a commitment, versus paying On-Demand for the remainder) and **utilization** (the fraction of the commitment you bought that is actually used, versus paying for idle committed capacity) continuously with Cost Explorer's Savings Plans and RI reports, not only at purchase time. And **ladder** commitments, staggering purchase terms and sizes over time, instead of one large bet on a single forecast that may not hold for 1-3 years. Spot remains a separate, complementary tool: layering Spot under a Savings Plan baseline for variable, interruption-tolerant demand captures a steep discount on the portion of usage a fixed-term commitment fits badly.

sections.heading: The Classic Bill-Shock Pattern: Forgot to Turn It Off
sections.body:
Many of the most surprising and avoidable AWS bills share one root cause: something kept running, or kept existing, long after anyone needed it, and nobody was watching for that. It shows up in a few recurring shapes. A **development or test environment** (an EC2 fleet and an RDS instance) built to match production and left running 24/7 although it is used only 9-to-6 on weekdays: that is 168 hours a week paid for against about 45 used, roughly 3.7 times more than needed. An **unattached EBS volume** left behind after its instance was terminated (a root volume is deleted with the instance by default, but additional volumes are kept unless configured otherwise) accrues storage cost indefinitely. An **idle Elastic IP address**: AWS charges for public IPv4 addresses by the hour, and since February 2024 that applies to every public IPv4 address, in use or not, so an unassociated one is pure waste that surprises people who assume a 'reserved but unused' resource is free. **Orphaned EBS snapshots**, taken as routine backups and never cleaned up, pile up for years past any retention need. And an easy one to miss: a **NAT Gateway** left provisioned for an environment decommissioned in every other respect, still billing by the hour (and per GB processed) for a resource nothing routes through.

None of these needs anyone to do something wrong. Each is the residue of infrastructure that was correctly created for a purpose, correctly stopped being used, and never decommissioned. That is why the pattern persists: it takes the absence of a cleanup step, not a mistake, and unlike most technical debt the cost accrues every hour without anyone touching anything.

sections.heading: Tagging: Making Spend Attributable, Not Just Visible
sections.body:
The guardrails below depend on a prerequisite: knowing *whose* spend is *whose*. Raw billing data groups cost by service and Region, not by team, environment, or project. That needs **cost allocation tags**, key/value pairs (like `Environment=dev`, `Team=payments`, `Project=checkout-redesign`) attached to resources at creation and then activated in the Billing console so Cost Explorer and Cost and Usage Reports can group and filter by them (activation can take up to 24 hours to take effect). Untagged spend is a governance blind spot: when the bill jumps, 'which team or project caused this' can't be answered for untagged resources, forcing a slow reconstruction from resource names, launch timestamps, and CloudTrail history instead of a Cost Explorer filter.

The practical fix is enforcing tags at creation time instead of retrofitting them: a tag policy, an AWS Config rule that flags untagged resources, or a Service Control Policy that denies creation calls missing required tags. Tagging that relies on everyone remembering tends to erode exactly when it matters, during an incident or rushed deployment. A small, consistently enforced tag set (Environment, Team, Project, at minimum) turns 'why did the bill jump' from a forensic investigation into a two-minute Cost Explorer query, and makes it possible to answer 'is dev really costing as much as prod', which is otherwise hard to answer with confidence.

sections.heading: Guardrails: Budgets, Anomaly Detection, and Scheduled Shutdowns Working Together
sections.body: Catching these patterns before next month's invoice takes a small layered set of automated guardrails, each catching a different failure shape. **AWS Budgets** sets a spending threshold (overall, or scoped to a tag, service, or account) and notifies you, or with **budget actions** triggers a response such as applying a restrictive IAM policy or stopping specific EC2/RDS instances, when actual or forecasted spend crosses it. It is a blunt but effective backstop for 'are we broadly on track this month'. **Cost Anomaly Detection** is finer-grained: instead of a fixed threshold it learns your normal day-to-day spend per service or account and alerts on a statistically unusual deviation, which catches a sudden spike (an oversized instance launched by a test script) well before it trips a monthly budget. For the common 'forgot to turn it off' pattern in non-production environments, the most direct fix is automation that doesn't rely on memory: a scheduled EventBridge rule invoking a small Lambda function (or AWS's Instance Scheduler solution) that stops tagged non-production instances outside business hours and starts them each morning, turning a 24/7 cost into roughly a weekday 9-to-6 one.

examples.title: A Nightly EventBridge Schedule That Stops Non-Production Instances Automatically
examples.explanation: This function is meant to be invoked by an EventBridge scheduled rule at 7pm on weekdays. It filters EC2 instances by the `Environment=dev` or `Environment=test` tag, among those currently running, and stops every match. A rule scheduled for 7am on weekdays would call `start_instances` on the same filtered set. It targets the bill-shock pattern of a non-production environment left running 24/7 although used roughly 9-to-6, and automating the shutdown removes the dependency on someone remembering. The mechanism depends on the `Environment` tag being present and correct: an untagged dev instance is invisible to the filter and keeps running. Two practical notes: the Lambda's role needs `ec2:DescribeInstances` and `ec2:StopInstances`, and EventBridge cron expressions run in UTC, so convert the 7pm to your time zone (EventBridge Scheduler supports time zones directly).

examples.title: Finding Idle, Unattached, and Orphaned Resources With the CLI
examples.code:
# Unattached EBS volumes -- still billing for storage, attached to nothing
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available \
  --query "Volumes[].{Id:VolumeId,SizeGiB:Size,Created:CreateTime}"

# Elastic IPs not associated with any running instance -- billed for being idle
aws ec2 describe-addresses \
  --query "Addresses[?AssociationId==null].{IP:PublicIp,AllocationId:AllocationId}"

# Snapshots older than 180 days -- candidates for review before assuming they're still needed
aws ec2 describe-snapshots --owner-ids self \
  --query "Snapshots[?StartTime<='2026-02-14'].{Id:SnapshotId,SizeGiB:VolumeSize,Created:StartTime}"
examples.explanation: None of these three queries looks for anything broken. They look for resources that are fine but have stopped serving a purpose. The first finds EBS volumes in the `available` state: they exist and bill for storage but are attached to nothing, which typically happens when an instance is terminated without deleting its non-root volumes. The second finds Elastic IPs with no `AssociationId`, not attached to an instance or network interface; AWS bills public IPv4 addresses hourly, so this idle state is pure waste. The third lists snapshots older than a cutoff (the date here is illustrative; compute it from today's date in a script). That doesn't make them safe to delete, since some may be needed for compliance, but they deserve a deliberate keep-or-delete decision. Running queries like these periodically, or better, as a scheduled report, catches the pattern before an invoice does. Note that each command covers only the current Region, so loop over Regions for a full picture.

examples.title: An AWS Budget With an Automatic Action, Not Just a Notification
examples.explanation: This budget is scoped to spend tagged `Environment=dev`, which is possible only because those resources were tagged consistently, tying back to the tagging discussion. Set at $500/month with a notification at 100% of the threshold, it is sized to catch the dev environment ballooning into a second production, instead of one account-wide budget that can't distinguish 'dev costs spiked' from 'prod grew because the business grew'. In the CLI the budget and its notifications are passed as two arguments (`--budget` and `--notifications-with-subscribers` of `aws budgets create-budget`), shown here in one document for readability, and the tag must be an activated cost allocation tag. Beyond a plain notification, AWS Budgets supports budget actions that apply a restrictive IAM policy or stop specific EC2/RDS instances once a threshold is crossed, turning a passive alert into a guardrail that acts on its own.

misconceptions.description: Once you've purchased Reserved Instances or a Savings Plan for your steady-state fleet, your infrastructure cost is now fixed and doesn't need further monitoring.
misconceptions.clarification: A commitment covers usage up to what was purchased. If actual usage later exceeds it, the excess is billed at On-Demand rates on top; if usage drops (a service shrinks, migrates to a different instance family, or is decommissioned), you keep paying for the unused portion for the rest of the term. Ongoing coverage and utilization tracking (Cost Explorer's Savings Plans and RI reports) is necessary because a commitment doesn't resize itself to match usage the way On-Demand billing does.

misconceptions.description: The AWS bill only grows when someone actively launches new resources, so if nobody is doing that, spend should stay flat.
misconceptions.clarification: Many common resources keep accruing cost with no effort from anyone: an unattached EBS volume left after its instance was terminated, an idle Elastic IP, a NAT Gateway still provisioned for a decommissioned environment, and snapshots nobody revisits all keep billing without any new resource being launched. This is the 'forgot to turn it off' pattern: spend growing, or failing to shrink, from the absence of a cleanup step, not from any new action.

exercises.prompt: A monthly cost review shows the dev environment costing almost exactly as much as the production environment, even though the team only actively uses dev during roughly 45 out of the 168 hours in a week (9am-6pm, Monday-Friday). Diagnose why dev costs so much relative to its actual usage, and estimate the rough savings a fix would produce.
exercises.code:
environment  instance_hours_billed_per_month  monthly_cost
prod         2 x 730 hours = 1460               $290
dev          2 x 730 hours = 1460               $290
# dev is only actually used ~45 hours/week x ~4.3 weeks/month = ~194 hours/month
hints: Compare instance_hours_billed against actual usage hours for dev: what fraction of the 1460 billed hours do the 194 actual-use hours represent?
The instances themselves aren't necessarily oversized (that would be a right-sizing question) -- focus on whether they need to be running at all outside the hours anyone uses them.
Think about the specific automation from this concept's explanation that directly targets exactly this pattern -- running non-production infrastructure only during the hours it's actually used.
exercises.solutionCode:
# Automate a stop/start schedule for dev instances outside business hours,
# e.g. via an EventBridge rule + Lambda (see the earlier example), or AWS's
# Instance Scheduler solution, tagged Environment=dev

# Rough savings estimate:
# actual usage ~194 hours/month out of 1460 billed hours/month
# -> billing roughly 194/1460 = ~13% of current dev hours instead of 100%
# -> dev cost drops from ~$290/month toward roughly $290 * 0.13 ~= $38/month
# (ignoring any per-instance-hour minimums or non-compute costs that don't scale down)
exercises.solutionExplanation: Dev is billed for the same 1460 instance-hours per month as prod (2 instances running continuously, 730 hours each) although it is used for only about 194 of them, roughly 13%. This is the 24/7-for-a-9-to-6 pattern: nothing need be oversized or misconfigured per instance, the instances just never stop outside working hours. The fix is a scheduled stop/start (an EventBridge-triggered Lambda, or Instance Scheduler) targeting the dev tag, stopping instances each evening and starting them each weekday morning. EC2 On-Demand compute is billed per second while running and not at all while stopped, so cutting billed hours from 1460 to about 194 should cut dev compute cost by a similar proportion, from about $290 toward $38 a month, with no change to the instances, only to when they run. EBS volumes and Elastic IPs on stopped instances keep billing, so the real saving is somewhat smaller. (A stopped RDS instance restarts automatically after 7 days, so schedule it rather than stopping it once.)

exercises.prompt: Write a boto3 (Python) script that finds every EBS volume in the 'available' (unattached) state across the account and prints its volume ID, size, and age in days, so a team can review them before deciding what to delete.
hints: describe_volumes accepts a Filters argument -- filter on Name='status', Values=['available'] to get only unattached volumes.
Each volume dict in the response includes 'VolumeId', 'Size' (GiB), and 'CreateTime' (a timezone-aware datetime).
Subtract CreateTime from the current UTC time (datetime.now(timezone.utc)) to get a timedelta, then use .days for a whole-number age.
exercises.solutionCode:
import boto3
from datetime import datetime, timezone

ec2 = boto3.client("ec2")

def find_unattached_volumes():
    response = ec2.describe_volumes(
        Filters=[{"Name": "status", "Values": ["available"]}]
    )
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    for volume in response["Volumes"]:
        age_days = (now - volume["CreateTime"]).days
        print(f"{volume['VolumeId']}  {volume['Size']}GiB  age={age_days}d")

find_unattached_volumes()
exercises.solutionExplanation: The `Filters=[{"Name": "status", "Values": ["available"]}]` argument restricts `describe_volumes` to only volumes in the `available` state, which means they exist and bill for storage but are not attached to any instance, the unattached-volume waste from the explanation. For each match, `volume["Size"]` is the provisioned size in GiB (which determines storage cost), and subtracting `volume["CreateTime"]` from the current UTC time gives a `timedelta` whose `.days` is the age. Age helps a team decide whether a volume unattached for 400 days is safe to delete or one from yesterday might be mid-migration (`CreateTime` is when the volume was created, not when it was detached, so it is only a rough guide). The script reports candidates and deletes nothing: an unattached volume isn't necessarily safe to delete without a human confirming, so automating discovery while keeping deletion manual is a conservative default. `describe_volumes` returns up to a page of results, so use a paginator (`ec2.get_paginator("describe_volumes")`) for accounts with many volumes.

assessments.prompt: A finance team notices AWS spend jumped noticeably last Tuesday, in a way that's still comfortably under the monthly budget threshold everyone monitors. Which tool is specifically designed to catch a spike like this quickly, rather than waiting for it to accumulate into a budget breach?
options: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, since it learns normal day-to-day spend patterns and flags statistically unusual deviations, independent of any fixed monthly threshold.
AWS Budgets, since it tracks monthly spend against a threshold.
Resource tagging, since it makes spend attributable to a specific team or project.
Savings Plans coverage reports, since they show how much of current usage is covered by a commitment, and any drop in that coverage figure is a reliable sign that spending has become unusual.
assessments.explanation: The scenario describes a sudden day-level spike that hasn't yet accumulated enough to breach a monthly budget, the gap AWS Budgets (“AWS Budgets, since it tracks monthly spend…”) is poorly suited to catch quickly, since it's fundamentally a threshold-over-a-period tool, not a day-to-day pattern-deviation detector. Cost Anomaly Detection is purpose-built for precisely this case: it models expected day-to-day spend and alerts on a statistically unusual deviation as soon as it happens, regardless of whether the monthly total is anywhere near a budget limit yet. Tagging (“Resource tagging, since it makes spend attributable…”) helps attribute spend once you're investigating, but doesn't itself detect or flag anything unusual. Savings Plans coverage reports (“Savings Plans coverage reports, since they show…”) are about commitment utilization, unrelated to detecting an unexpected spend spike.

assessments.prompt: A team allocates an Elastic IP address for a planned migration, but the migration is delayed, leaving the IP unattached to any running instance for several weeks. Do they pay anything for this?
options: Yes, but only if the account has fewer than five total Elastic IP addresses allocated.

Yes -- AWS specifically charges an hourly rate for an Elastic IP that isn't associated with a running instance, precisely to discourage indefinitely holding a scarce public IPv4 address without actually using it.
No, Elastic IP addresses are always free regardless of whether they're attached to a running instance.
No, Elastic IPs are only ever billed once actually associated with an instance; unattached time is always free.
assessments.explanation: AWS charges for an idle, unassociated Elastic IP, one of the easy-to-miss bill-shock patterns: a resource that looks 'reserved but unused' and so intuitively free is billed, in part to discourage squatting on scarce public IPv4 space. (Since February 2024, AWS bills every public IPv4 address hourly, whether or not it is in use.) The “No, Elastic IP addresses are always free…” and “No, Elastic IPs are only ever billed…” options both assume the intuitive-but-incorrect 'unused should be free' framing. The “Yes, but only if the account has…” option invents a count-based exemption threshold that doesn't reflect how this charge actually works -- it applies based on association status, not total IP count.

assessments.prompt: A monthly bill shows a $4,000 increase, and the finance team wants to know which team or project is responsible. Most of the newly created resources involved were never tagged with Environment, Team, or Project tags. What is the most direct consequence of this, and the recommended fix going forward?
options: Nothing; AWS billing automatically attributes all spend to the IAM user who created each resource, regardless of whether it was tagged.
This only matters for resources billed under a Savings Plan; On-Demand spend is always automatically attributed by account structure alone.

The increase can't be broken down by team or project using Cost Explorer's tag-based filtering, forcing a slow, manual reconstruction from resource names, launch timestamps, and CloudTrail history instead; the recommended fix is enforcing tagging at creation time -- via a tagging policy, an AWS Config rule, or a Service Control Policy -- rather than relying on everyone remembering to tag consistently.
Nothing can be done retroactively or going forward; once a resource is created untagged, AWS permanently loses any ability to ever attribute its cost.
assessments.explanation: Untagged spend is exactly the governance blind spot described: without cost allocation tags, Cost Explorer has no team/project dimension to filter or group by for that spend, turning a two-minute query into a slow, manual investigation using whatever weaker signals (resource names, timestamps, CloudTrail) happen to be available. The fix is enforcing tagging at creation time through policy mechanisms, since relying purely on individual discipline tends to fail during exactly the rushed situations where good tagging matters most. The “Nothing; AWS billing automatically attributes all spend…” option invents automatic IAM-based attribution that Cost Explorer's tag-based grouping does not provide. The “Nothing can be done retroactively or going…” option overstates the permanence of the problem -- resources can still be tagged retroactively going forward, even if past unattributed spend can't be reconstructed precisely. The “This only matters for resources billed under…” option fabricates an arbitrary restriction to Savings Plans that has no basis; tagging and attribution apply identically to On-Demand spend.

assessments.prompt: A colleague says: 'We should just pick the biggest, most reserved-capacity-covered instances everywhere -- bigger is safer, and reserved is cheaper.' Explain what's wrong with applying this as a blanket rule, and describe the actual reasoning process you'd use instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Both halves of that rule skip the step that determines whether they help: looking at usage data. 'Bigger is safer' assumes more capacity can only be good, but an oversized instance at 15% CPU isn't safer than a correctly sized one at 60-70%. It pays for headroom that is never used, with no reliability benefit. Right-sizing from CloudWatch utilization data (and tools like Compute Optimizer that automate the analysis) finds the mismatch between provisioned and used capacity instead of treating bigger as a free safety margin. (Some headroom for peaks and failover is sensible; the point is to size it deliberately, not by default.) 'Reserved is cheaper' is true only for usage that is steady and predictable for the whole term. Applied blanket-wide, including to workloads still being validated or with variable demand, it risks over-committing: paying for reserved capacity that goes unused because the workload shrank, moved to another instance family, or never needed that much, with no way out of the remaining term. The better process is to separate the two decisions and apply real data to each: first, right-size based on actual observed utilization, choosing an instance family and size that matches the genuine bottleneck (CPU, memory, or otherwise) rather than defaulting to bigger; second, and only for the resulting right-sized footprint, apply a pricing model matched to that specific workload's predictability -- Reserved/Savings Plans for the portion that's demonstrably steady-state and long-lived, On-Demand for anything still being validated or genuinely variable, and Spot for anything stateless and interruption-tolerant. Treating 'bigger' and 'reserved' as universal defaults skips exactly the analysis that would tell you whether either one is actually buying anything in a given case.

assessments.prompt: Your team's AWS bill doubled last month and finance wants an explanation by Friday. Describe how you would find the cause and what you would put in place so it does not happen silently again.
assessments.modelAnswer: Start in Cost Explorer grouped by service, then by usage type, account and tag, comparing with the previous month to find which line items grew (daily granularity shows the day the curve bent). Common culprits are NAT gateway data processing, cross-AZ or internet data transfer, forgotten EC2 or RDS instances, unattached EBS volumes and snapshots, and verbose CloudWatch logs. Use resource tags to map the spend to a team or feature, and check deploy history for what changed when the curve bent. Fix the immediate waste (stop or rightsize idle resources, add S3 lifecycle rules, set log retention), and consider Savings Plans for steady load. To prevent a repeat, enforce cost-allocation tags, set AWS Budgets with alerts per account or team, enable anomaly detection, and review cost as part of design reviews rather than only when the bill arrives.
